narration.text: Picture yourself outside on a perfect, sunlit day — then the Sun’s disk in the sky is simply gone. Do we immediately drop off the planet? Freeze in an instant? Do the planets scatter like shrapnel? We'll follow a physical clock — seconds, minutes, hours, days, months and years — and at each tick show the mechanism that controls that timescale: the finite travel time of signals from the Sun, Earth's thermal inertia that slows cooling, and orbital inertia that governs motion once the Sun's pull no longer arrives. Those mechanisms answer the visceral questions and set up the detailed timelines we'll return to.

compiledScenePrompt.positivePrompt:
[SCENE TASK]
story scene shot for a 2D animated documentary. This is a finished cinematic scene, NOT a character reference sheet or model sheet — do not arrange multiple views/panels, do not use a plain studio background, do not compose a turnaround.

[STYLE LOCK]
STYLE LOCK — Classic 2D Documentary. Colored 2D documentary illustration. Linework: confident black silhouette outlines, finer interior lines. Shading: flat cel shading, 1–2 tonal steps; no gradients. Texture: subtle uniform paper grain. Palette: 2–4 restrained colored hues plus neutrals, never uncolored line art. Proportions: rounded simplified adult forms, expressive economical faces, not chibi. Lighting: motivated directional light, soft shadows. Perspective: coherent one/two-point, grounded eye level. Do not: photographic realism, 3D, anime, preschool cartoon or corporate vector art.

[COMPOSITION]
Shot size: MEDIUM. Eye-level three-quarter view of the subject in its environment
Focal point: Earth.

[CURRENT ACTION / CONTENT]
Show Earth in daylight, then the Sun's disk suddenly missing, and present the three visceral questions to set stakes and create curiosity.

[LOCATION]
Earth (daylit hemisphere)

[WORLD STATE]
- timeOfDay: daylight_hemisphere
- sun_disk_visible: true

[SEMANTIC REQUIREMENTS]
MUST SHOW: Earth in daylight; Sun's disk visually removed; Three question captions (feel it? freeze? fly away?)
MUST NOT SHOW: Explosive or cinematic destruction of the Sun; Immediate visual of Earth being flung away

[RENDER RULES]
Colored illustration, never uncolored line art or a monochrome technical plate. Never a character reference sheet or turnaround. Displays stay blank or abstract; exact lettering is added afterward.

stylePayload.name: Classic 2D Documentary
stylePayload.summary: Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
stylePayload.linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
stylePayload.shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
stylePayload.texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
stylePayload.palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
stylePayload.faceConstruction: Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.
stylePayload.bodyProportions: Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
stylePayload.environmentDetail: Moderately detailed, readable environments and props with clear foreground/midground/background separation. Purposeful, uncluttered set-dressing — every visible object should feel intentional.
stylePayload.lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
stylePayload.perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.
stylePayload.diagramGrammar: Diagrams use the same bold linework/palette as narrative scenes, never a generic flat corporate-infographic look. Labels and callouts are added programmatically in the video layer — never baked into the image.
stylePayload.mapGrammar: Maps use a hand-illustrated cartographic style, not literally aged/parchment unless the topic calls for it. Place names and route lines are added programmatically — never baked into the image.
negativeConstraints: not generic corporate flat vector art

stylePayload.name: Classic 2D Documentary
stylePayload.summary: Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
stylePayload.linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
stylePayload.shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
stylePayload.texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
stylePayload.palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
stylePayload.faceConstruction: Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.
stylePayload.bodyProportions: Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
stylePayload.environmentDetail: Moderately detailed, readable environments and props with clear foreground/midground/background separation. Purposeful, uncluttered set-dressing — every visible object should feel intentional.
stylePayload.lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
stylePayload.perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.
stylePayload.diagramGrammar: Diagrams use the same bold linework/palette as narrative scenes, never a generic flat corporate-infographic look. Labels and callouts are added programmatically in the video layer — never baked into the image.

narration.text: Movies love instant, planet‑wide catastrophe — oceans leaping off Earth, people flung into space, an immediate global freeze — but the physics disagrees. The reason is concrete: light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach us (varying by ±~9 s through the year), and changes in gravity propagate at the same finite speed. So a sudden change at the Sun cannot push or darken us until that signal arrives. The immediate aftermath is therefore calm compared with cinema: for those minutes the system keeps behaving as if nothing happened.

narration.text: Movies love instant, planet‑wide catastrophe — oceans leaping off Earth, people flung into space, an immediate global freeze — but the physics disagrees. The reason is concrete: light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach us (varying by ±~9 s through the year), and changes in gravity propagate at the same finite speed. So a sudden change at the Sun cannot push or darken us until that signal arrives. The immediate aftermath is therefore calm compared with cinema: for those minutes the system keeps behaving as if nothing happened.

narration.text: If the Sun were to vanish this instant, Earth wouldn't register it for about 499 seconds — roughly 8 minutes 19 seconds — because information (light or changes in gravity) has to travel here. Practically that means: photons already en route keep lighting our skies until that delay elapses, and the local gravitational field still reflects the Sun as it was eight minutes earlier. references.promptSnapshot:
[STYLE LOCK]
Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
Linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
Shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
Texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
Palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
Lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
Perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.

[ENTITY IDENTITY]
Sun (stellar disk / central mass): A self-luminous stellar disk: near-circular, very bright white–yellow disk with subtle limb darkening (center slightly brighter than edge) and granulation-level texture implied by fine mottling (no photographic microdetail). Disk color leans white with mild warm (yellow) tint at lower saturations for illustration. No persistent corona visible while the photosphere is shown; when corona is illustrated it must only appear in contexts where the photosphere is blanked/occluded (eclipse-style). Scale: disk dominates its own frame region and is the primary light source in space views. Do not depict physical disappearance effects (e.g., instantaneous gravitational waves reaching Earth) before the light-time delay.

[REQUESTED VIEW]
canonical celestial view — Canonical celestial appearance reference.
One subject: the Sun only. The canonical, immediately recognizable appearance of this celestial body alone.
Astronomically plausible scale, lighting and color for how this body actually appears.
NO people, spacecraft, vehicles, unrelated planets, moons, orbit arrows, diagrams, labels, scale bars or explanatory callouts.

[PROPORTION / SHAPE RULES]
Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.

[BACKGROUND / CANONICAL ASSET]
Plain, seamless, muted neutral studio background ONLY — no room, no furniture, no environment of any kind, no walls, no floor detail, no location-specific geometry. CHARACTER and OBJECT identity must be established completely independent of any location — locations are established separately by their own location references. Clear subject silhouette, full subject visible with margins. No scenic distractions or dramatic cropping.

[CANONICAL REFERENCE NEGATIVE CONTRACT]
- NO infographic layout, explainer board, presentation board, educational poster, diagram, arrows, callouts or annotations
- NO collage, split screen, contact sheet, multi-panel layout, duplicate subject, repeated copies or alternate views in one image
- NO readable text, labels, captions, legends, logos, UI, numbers, symbols posing as text or watermarks
- NO narrative action, before/after comparison, process sequence or finished story scene
- not hyper-realistic / photographic
- not childish preschool cartoon
- not generic corporate flat vector art
- no 3D-render look
- no anime/manga stylization
- Depicting a bright, extended corona simultaneously with an unobstructed photosphere (corona-visible-only during occultation)
- Showing any causal effect on Earth (illumination or gravity) before the ~499 s propagation delay
- readable text
- letters
- numbers
- names
- identification badge lettering
- logo typography
- logos
- badges containing lettering
- signage
- numerical displays
- labels
- watermark
- generated UI copy
- captions
- letters or numbers of any kind rendered into the image

referenceLeakRisk.risk: Reference pixels are supplied. Character prompts constrain identity versus pose; non-character references do not consistently include an explicit instruction against copying source composition, layout, or embedded text.

narration.text: If the Sun were to vanish this instant, Earth wouldn't register it for about 499 seconds — roughly 8 minutes 19 seconds — because information (light or changes in gravity) has to travel here. Practically that means: photons already en route keep lighting our skies until that delay elapses, and the local gravitational field still reflects the Sun as it was eight minutes earlier. During those eight minutes nothing at the Sun can causally change what we see or feel here, so the planet carries on — sunlight keeps arriving and Earth continues on its orbital motion — until the trailing edge of that information finally arrives.

references.promptSnapshot:
[STYLE LOCK]
Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
Linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
Shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
Texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
Palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
Lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
Perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.

[ENTITY IDENTITY]
Sun (stellar disk / central mass): A self-luminous stellar disk: near-circular, very bright white–yellow disk with subtle limb darkening (center slightly brighter than edge) and granulation-level texture implied by fine mottling (no photographic microdetail). Disk color leans white with mild warm (yellow) tint at lower saturations for illustration. No persistent corona visible while the photosphere is shown; when corona is illustrated it must only appear in contexts where the photosphere is blanked/occluded (eclipse-style). Scale: disk dominates its own frame region and is the primary light source in space views. Do not depict physical disappearance effects (e.g., instantaneous gravitational waves reaching Earth) before the light-time delay.

[REQUESTED VIEW]
canonical celestial view — Canonical celestial appearance reference.
One subject: the Sun only. The canonical, immediately recognizable appearance of this celestial body alone.
Astronomically plausible scale, lighting and color for how this body actually appears.
NO people, spacecraft, vehicles, unrelated planets, moons, orbit arrows, diagrams, labels, scale bars or explanatory callouts.

[PROPORTION / SHAPE RULES]

narration.text: If the Sun were to vanish this instant, Earth wouldn't register it for about 499 seconds — roughly 8 minutes 19 seconds — because information (light or changes in gravity) has to travel here. Practically that means: photons already en route keep lighting our skies until that delay elapses, and the local gravitational field still reflects the Sun as it was eight minutes earlier. During those eight minutes nothing at the Sun can causally change what we see or feel here, so the planet carries on — sunlight keeps arriving and Earth continues on its orbital motion — until the trailing edge of that information finally arrives.

narration.text: If the Sun were to vanish this instant, Earth wouldn't register it for about 499 seconds — roughly 8 minutes 19 seconds — because information (light or changes in gravity) has to travel here. narration.text: But even though the direct beam ends in a blink, the sky doesn't go fully black at once. The atmosphere scatters sunlight — Rayleigh scattering off molecules and Mie scattering from aerosols — so diffuse skylight persists. references.promptSnapshot:
[STYLE LOCK]
Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
Linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
Shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
Texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
Palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
Lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
Perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.
Project-specific mood: Desaturated, cool-blue documentary palette with restrained warm highlights for remaining sunlight; clean, high-contrast scientific illustration lines and subtle textured shading (no photoreal photographic texture).

[ENTITY IDENTITY]
Local sky / atmosphere: A local sky column from horizon to zenith: color graded from warm, bright scattering near the sunward horizon to cooler desaturated blue higher up and toward the anti-sunward sky, transitioning to near-black space above the atmosphere. Include visible Rayleigh blue hue at shorter scattering paths and paler, desaturated orange/pink tones in low-sun geometries. Represent multiple scattering paths with soft diffuse glow near horizon (twilight band). Texture: soft gradients and subtle aerosol haze layer near horizon; no hard edges. Scale: vertical column spanning frame height in horizon compositions.

[REQUESTED VIEW]
Camera anchor: wide horizon — Storyboard camera anchor: wide_horizon.
A reusable empty animation set from this exact camera anchor. Show continuous floor, walls/terrain, ceiling or sky structure and fixed spatial landmarks in a coherent perspective from this specific angle.
Preserve the canonical room/location layout exactly as established for this location — this must be recognizably the SAME place from a different angle, not a new location.
NO recurring characters and no people of any kind, unless the location's own canonical spec explicitly requires one for scale — the location itself is the subject.

[PROPORTION / SHAPE RULES]
Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.

[BACKGROUND / CANONICAL ASSET]
A reusable empty animation set from the requested storyboard camera anchor. Show continuous floor, walls, ceiling structure and fixed spatial landmarks in a coherent wide perspective. Preserve the canonical room layout. No people, no cutaway or floating room, no studio background.

referenceLeakRisk.risk: Reference pixels are supplied. Character prompts constrain identity versus pose; non-character references do not consistently include an explicit instruction against copying source composition, layout, or embedded text.

narration.text: But even though the direct beam ends in a blink, the sky doesn't go fully black at once. The atmosphere scatters sunlight — Rayleigh scattering off molecules and Mie scattering from aerosols — so diffuse skylight persists. That gives us a twilight-like decay that can last from tens of seconds up to many minutes, and in very clear, low‑light places it can take tens of minutes before you reach true night. How long depends on where the Sun was in the sky, how dusty the air is, and local light pollution. So there’s an abrupt loss of direct sun, layered on top of a slower decay of sky brightness.

narration.text: But even though the direct beam ends in a blink, the sky doesn't go fully black at once. The atmosphere scatters sunlight — Rayleigh scattering off molecules and Mie scattering from aerosols — so diffuse skylight persists. That gives us a twilight-like decay that can last from tens of seconds up to many minutes, and in very clear, low‑light places it can take tens of minutes before you reach true night. How long depends on where the Sun was in the sky, how dusty the air is, and local light pollution. So there’s an abrupt loss of direct sun, layered on top of a slower decay of sky brightness.

The atmosphere scatters sunlight — Rayleigh scattering off molecules and Mie scattering from aerosols — so diffuse skylight persists. That gives us a twilight-like decay that can last from tens of seconds up to many minutes, and in very clear, low‑light places it can take tens of minutes before you reach true night. How long depends on where the Sun was in the sky, how dusty the air is, and local light pollution. So there’s an abrupt loss of direct sun, layered on top of a slower decay of sky brightness.

Local sky / atmosphere: A local sky column from horizon to zenith: color graded from warm, bright scattering near the sunward horizon to cooler desaturated blue higher up and toward the anti-sunward sky, transitioning to near-black space above the atmosphere. Include visible Rayleigh blue hue at shorter scattering paths and paler, desaturated orange/pink tones in low-sun geometries. Represent multiple scattering paths with soft diffuse glow near horizon (twilight band). Texture: soft gradients and subtle aerosol haze layer near horizon; no hard edges. Scale: vertical column spanning frame height in horizon compositions.

A reusable empty animation set from this exact camera anchor. Show continuous floor, walls/terrain, ceiling or sky structure and fixed spatial landmarks in a coherent perspective from this specific angle.
Preserve the canonical room/location layout exactly as established for this location — this must be recognizably the SAME place from a different angle, not a new location.

references.promptSnapshot:
[STYLE LOCK]
Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
Linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
Shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
Texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
Palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
Lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
Perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.
Project-specific mood: Desaturated, cool-blue documentary palette with restrained warm highlights for remaining sunlight; clean, high-contrast scientific illustration lines and subtle textured shading (no photoreal photographic texture).

[ENTITY IDENTITY]
Local sky / atmosphere: A local sky column from horizon to zenith: color graded from warm, bright scattering near the sunward horizon to cooler desaturated blue higher up and toward the anti-sunward sky, transitioning to near-black space above the atmosphere. Include visible Rayleigh blue hue at shorter scattering paths and paler, desaturated orange/pink tones in low-sun geometries. Represent multiple scattering paths with soft diffuse glow near horizon (twilight band). Texture: soft gradients and subtle aerosol haze layer near horizon; no hard edges. Scale: vertical column spanning frame height in horizon compositions.

[REQUESTED VIEW]
Camera anchor: wide horizon — Storyboard camera anchor: wide_horizon.
A reusable empty animation set from this exact camera anchor. Show continuous floor, walls/terrain, ceiling or sky structure and fixed spatial landmarks in a coherent perspective from this specific angle.

narration.text: Inside a few seconds to a few minutes, machines and biological systems react. Grid-connected inverters and protective relays that rely on solar input typically detect a sudden loss and can trip or change modes on timescales of under a handful of seconds, which can create immediate frequency and voltage excursions on the power grid. At the same time, the tiny molecular machinery of photosynthesis shuts down extremely fast — electron transport and fluorescence signals collapse in milliseconds to seconds — while whole-leaf adjustments like stomatal movement take tens of seconds to minutes to begin responding. Those device- and plant-level timescales give us a practical short-window timeline: 0–1 s for beam loss and detector response, 1–10 s for fast electronic and biochemical transients, 10 s–1 min for twilight and early biological adjustment, and 1–10 min for short thermal and grid stabilization steps.

Grid-connected inverters and protective relays that rely on solar input typically detect a sudden loss and can trip or change modes on timescales of under a handful of seconds, which can create immediate frequency and voltage excursions on the power grid. narration.text: Inside a few seconds to a few minutes, machines and biological systems react. Grid-connected inverters and protective relays that rely on solar input typically detect a sudden loss and can trip or change modes on timescales of under a handful of seconds, which can create immediate frequency and voltage excursions on the power grid. stylePayload.summary: Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
stylePayload.linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
stylePayload.shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
stylePayload.texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
stylePayload.palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
stylePayload.faceConstruction: Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.
stylePayload.bodyProportions: Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
stylePayload.environmentDetail: Moderately detailed, readable environments and props with clear foreground/midground/background separation. Purposeful, uncluttered set-dressing — every visible object should feel intentional.
stylePayload.lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
stylePayload.perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.

narration.text: Inside a few seconds to a few minutes, machines and biological systems react. Grid-connected inverters and protective relays that rely on solar input typically detect a sudden loss and can trip or change modes on timescales of under a handful of seconds, which can create immediate frequency and voltage excursions on the power grid. At the same time, the tiny molecular machinery of photosynthesis shuts down extremely fast — electron transport and fluorescence signals collapse in milliseconds to seconds — while whole-leaf adjustments like stomatal movement take tens of seconds to minutes to begin responding. Those device- and plant-level timescales give us a practical short-window timeline: 0–1 s for beam loss and detector response, 1–10 s for fast electronic and biochemical transients, 10 s–1 min for twilight and early biological adjustment, and 1–10 min for short thermal and grid stabilization steps.

narration.text: Planets orbit because a central force continually bends their motion; remove that force and they stop curving and coast straight. Concretely, Earth moves at ≈29.8 km/s, so in the roughly 499‑second signal delay it travels about 15,000 km along its orbit; in one hour it would traverse ≈107,000 km. When the gravitational change finally reaches Earth, the instantaneous acceleration toward the Sun vanishes and Earth's path becomes a straight-line tangent to its previous orbit at that location. That doesn't fling Earth outward in an explosion — it simply converts curved orbital motion into inertial straight-line motion at the velocity it already had.

Concretely, Earth moves at ≈29.8 km/s, so in the roughly 499‑second signal delay it travels about 15,000 km along its orbit; in one hour it would traverse ≈107,000 km. story scene shot for a 2D animated documentary. This is a finished cinematic scene, NOT a character reference sheet or model sheet — do not arrange multiple views/panels, do not use a plain studio background, do not compose a turnaround.

[STYLE LOCK]
STYLE LOCK — Classic 2D Documentary. Colored 2D documentary illustration. Linework: confident black silhouette outlines, finer interior lines. Shading: flat cel shading, 1–2 tonal steps; no gradients. Texture: subtle uniform paper grain. Palette: 2–4 restrained colored hues plus neutrals, never uncolored line art. Proportions: rounded simplified adult forms, expressive economical faces, not chibi. Lighting: motivated directional light, soft shadows. Perspective: coherent one/two-point, grounded eye level. Do not: photographic realism, 3D, anime, preschool cartoon or corporate vector art.

[COMPOSITION]
Shot size: CLOSE. Close side view centered on the narrated action and its immediate result
Focal point: Earth.

[CURRENT ACTION / CONTENT]
Show Earth's orbit path then switch to a tangent straight-line trajectory at the moment gravity change arrives, with distance labels (≈15,000 km in ~8 min).

[LOCATION]
Earth (daylit hemisphere)

[WORLD STATE]
- frame_of_reference: heliocentric_fixed

[SEMANTIC REQUIREMENTS]
MUST SHOW: Orbit-to-tangent transition; Label with Earth speed ≈29.8 km/s and distance ≈15,000 km
MUST NOT SHOW: Immediate explosion or chaotic scattering at the moment signal arrives

[TEXT-SAFE COMPOSITION]
Leave clear, uncluttered visual space (upper or lower third) for a text overlay to be added afterward. Do not render any title, caption or heading yourself.

[RENDER RULES]
Colored illustration, never uncolored line art or a monochrome technical plate. Never a character reference sheet or turnaround. Displays stay blank or abstract; exact lettering is added afterward.

narration.text: Planets orbit because a central force continually bends their motion; remove that force and they stop curving and coast straight. Concretely, Earth moves at ≈29.8 km/s, so in the roughly 499‑second signal delay it travels about 15,000 km along its orbit; in one hour it would traverse ≈107,000 km. When the gravitational change finally reaches Earth, the instantaneous acceleration toward the Sun vanishes and Earth's path becomes a straight-line tangent to its previous orbit at that location. That doesn't fling Earth outward in an explosion — it simply converts curved orbital motion into inertial straight-line motion at the velocity it already had.

narration.text: Planets orbit because a central force continually bends their motion; remove that force and they stop curving and coast straight. Concretely, Earth moves at ≈29.8 km/s, so in the roughly 499‑second signal delay it travels about 15,000 km along its orbit; in one hour it would traverse ≈107,000 km. narration.text: The Moon is close enough that short-term dynamics keep it bound to Earth. Its orbital speed (~1.02 km/s) is below the escape speed at lunar distance (~1.4 km/s), so immediately after the Sun's influence is gone the Moon stays in Earth orbit rather than flying away. Over longer timescales — centuries to millennia — the two-body interaction with Earth plus perturbations from other bodies can nudge the system into a new configuration. Those long-term possibilities (slow drift inward or outward, temporary capture, or eventual escape) are highly sensitive to small changes in geometry and timing; trustworthy answers require full N‑body simulations.

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

[ENTITY IDENTITY]
Sun (stellar disk / central mass): A self-luminous stellar disk: near-circular, very bright white–yellow disk with subtle limb darkening (center slightly brighter than edge) and granulation-level texture implied by fine mottling (no photographic microdetail). Disk color leans white with mild warm (yellow) tint at lower saturations for illustration. No persistent corona visible while the photosphere is shown; when corona is illustrated it must only appear in contexts where the photosphere is blanked/occluded (eclipse-style). Scale: disk dominates its own frame region and is the primary light source in space views. Do not depict physical disappearance effects (e.g., instantaneous gravitational waves reaching Earth) before the light-time delay.

[REQUESTED VIEW]
canonical celestial view — Canonical celestial appearance reference.
One subject: the Sun only. The canonical, immediately recognizable appearance of this celestial body alone.
Astronomically plausible scale, lighting and color for how this body actually appears.
NO people, spacecraft, vehicles, unrelated planets, moons, orbit arrows, diagrams, labels, scale bars or explanatory callouts.

[PROPORTION / SHAPE RULES]
Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.

[BACKGROUND / CANONICAL ASSET]
Plain, seamless, muted neutral studio background ONLY — no room, no furniture, no environment of any kind, no walls, no floor detail, no location-specific geometry. CHARACTER and OBJECT identity must be established completely independent of any location — locations are established separately by their own location references. Clear subject silhouette, full subject visible with margins. No scenic distractions or dramatic cropping.

- NO infographic layout, explainer board, presentation board, educational poster, diagram, arrows, callouts or annotations

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

references.promptSnapshot:
[STYLE LOCK]
Bold 2D illustrated documentary style — thick confident outlines, rounded cartoon forms, and a restrained flat-shaded palette. Not hyper-realistic, not childish preschool cartoon, not generic corporate flat vector art.
Linework: Thick, confident black outlines on every silhouette edge, with lighter interior detail lines. No sketchy cross-hatching, no photorealistic edge rendering.
Shading: Restrained flat cel-shading, 1-2 tonal steps per surface (base, occasional shadow) — no painterly gradients, no hard outline on the shadow shapes themselves.
Texture: A light, uniform paper/canvas grain overlay across the whole image — subtle enough to never read as noise or damage, present enough to avoid a flat vector-art look.
Palette: Flat, readable hues — avoid neon/oversaturated color. Favor 2-4 dominant hues plus neutrals per scene so the image reads instantly, even at thumbnail size.
Lighting: Directional, motivated lighting with a clear implied light source and soft shadow shapes — never flat/shadowless, never harsh studio-flash lighting.
Perspective: Consistent one-to-two-point perspective per scene, eye-level or slightly low-angle by default for a grounded, cinematic feel.

[ENTITY IDENTITY]
Sun (stellar disk / central mass): A self-luminous stellar disk: near-circular, very bright white–yellow disk with subtle limb darkening (center slightly brighter than edge) and granulation-level texture implied by fine mottling (no photographic microdetail). Disk color leans white with mild warm (yellow) tint at lower saturations for illustration. No persistent corona visible while the photosphere is shown; when corona is illustrated it must only appear in contexts where the photosphere is blanked/occluded (eclipse-style). Scale: disk dominates its own frame region and is the primary light source in space views. Do not depict physical disappearance effects (e.g., instantaneous gravitational waves reaching Earth) before the light-time delay.

[REQUESTED VIEW]
canonical celestial view — Canonical celestial appearance reference.
One subject: the Sun only. The canonical, immediately recognizable appearance of this celestial body alone.
Astronomically plausible scale, lighting and color for how this body actually appears.
NO people, spacecraft, vehicles, unrelated planets, moons, orbit arrows, diagrams, labels, scale bars or explanatory callouts.

[PROPORTION / SHAPE RULES]
Rounded, slightly simplified cartoon proportions with strong, instantly-readable silhouettes — not chibi, not hyper-stylized anime.
Expressive but simple faces — economical linework for eyes/brows/mouth, clearly readable expression. Avoid hyper-detailed photographic facial rendering and avoid oversized preschool-cartoon eyes.

[BACKGROUND / CANONICAL ASSET]
Plain, seamless, muted neutral studio background ONLY — no room, no furniture, no environment of any kind, no walls, no floor detail, no location-specific geometry. CHARACTER and OBJECT identity must be established completely independent of any location — locations are established separately by their own location references. Clear subject silhouette, full subject visible with margins. No scenic distractions or dramatic cropping.

[CANONICAL REFERENCE NEGATIVE CONTRACT]
- NO infographic layout, explainer board, presentation board, educational poster, diagram, arrows, callouts or annotations
- NO collage, split screen, contact sheet, multi-panel layout, duplicate subject, repeated copies or alternate views in one image
- NO readable text, labels, captions, legends, logos, UI, numbers, symbols posing as text or watermarks
- NO narrative action, before/after comparison, process sequence or finished story scene
- not hyper-realistic / photographic
- not childish preschool cartoon
- not generic corporate flat vector art
- no 3D-render look
- no anime/manga stylization
- Depicting a bright, extended corona simultaneously with an unobstructed photosphere (corona-visible-only during occultation)
- Showing any causal effect on Earth (illumination or gravity) before the ~499 s propagation delay
- readable text
- letters
- numbers
- names
- identification badge lettering
- logo typography
- logos
- badges containing lettering
- signage
- numerical displays
- labels
- watermark
- generated UI copy
- captions
- letters or numbers of any kind rendered into the image

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

sketchContext.environment: Show a synthesized short timeline (0–1 s, 1–10 s, 10 s–1 min, 1–10 min, hours, days→weeks, months→years) mapping physical mechanisms to timescales: detector/PV response, inverter/grid actions, twilight scattering, atmospheric cooling, soil conduction, ocean mixed-layer loss. overclaim specific regional temperature numbers

factualVisualConstraints.description: Bucket timeline should align with F_practical_timeline_bucket_for_narration and F_direct_beam_and_detector_response for the fastest bins

narration.text: The instant the Sun's beam stops, Earth starts losing energy to space, but that loss is resisted by big thermal reservoirs. First, the atmosphere holds heat like a blanket: radiative cooling begins immediately but the air's heat capacity and vertical mixing mean surface temperatures fall only modestly in the first hours. Second, land surfaces release stored warmth more slowly — soils and rocks radiate and conduct heat downward over days to weeks. Third, the ocean mixed layer (the top tens of metres that exchange heat with the atmosphere) is a very large heat bank: its heat is drawn out over months to years, so coastal and sea-surface temperatures lag far behind the first atmospheric dip. Geothermal heat exists but is tiny compared to former solar input, so it cannot replace the Sun and deep cooling is ultimately inevitable. Precise regional numbers require full climate or mixed-layer model runs.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: At the microscopic level photosynthesis stops almost instantly: electron transport and fluorescence collapse within milliseconds to seconds once light ends. Whole leaves and plants then begin slower adjustments — stomata respond over seconds to minutes and carbohydrate redistribution follows over hours. That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

That means exposed crops and surface phytoplankton lose net productivity fastest (days to weeks), while large forests and soils buffer production for weeks to months. Electrically, satellites and spacecraft lose solar input immediately and switch to batteries; many small satellites can operate for hours to days before power runs out. Grid inverters and protection relays detect sudden solar loss in fractions of a second and trip or reconfigure within <1–5 s, while human operators and reserve dispatch unfold over minutes to hours. Whether communities survive beyond weeks or months depends on stored food, continuous power sources like nuclear or geothermal, and the resilience of supply chains — outcomes that need targeted engineering and logistical analysis.

narration.text: Out beyond Earth, anything relying on sunlight goes dark the instant the photons stop at its location; batteries and thermal control then set how long systems limp on. On planetary scales, removing the Sun's central force leaves the system in a delicate new balance: planets, moons and asteroids still interact with one another, and those mutual tugs — not a single dominant central mass — drive the long‑term evolution. Possible outcomes include captures, scattering, or ejections and, in rare cases, collisions; which of those plays out depends strongly on the exact geometry and timing of how the Sun's influence ended. Trustworthy predictions require dedicated N‑body integrations because small differences in initial conditions amplify over time, and we don't present numerical long‑term forecasts here.

narration.text: Here's a compact timeline to keep in your head. First: nothing changes locally for about eight minutes — then direct sunlight and solar power fall essentially to zero in under a second, though the sky fades more slowly over seconds to minutes as scattered light persists. Instruments and PV drop almost instantly, inverters/protections act in seconds and operator/reserve responses play out over minutes; photosynthesis collapses at molecular speed while whole plants and crops adjust over minutes to days. Thermally, temperatures begin falling immediately but do so over hours, days and then months because air, land and the ocean mixed layer store heat; mechanically, Earth will coast tangentally once the Sun's pull is gone and the Moon remains bound to Earth at first. The long‑term rearrangement of the Solar System — captures, escapes, collisions — is plausible but sensitive and requires N‑body modeling to predict.

narration.text: One last perspective: the first minutes look like almost nothing happened, and that's the point. The physics buys us that time because information can't travel faster than light. After that, darkness hits fast for direct light, machines and plants react quickly, temperatures fall more slowly because of stored heat, and orbital motion simply follows Newton's prescription once the central pull is removed. The real takeaway is a clean mental map: timescales are set by signal speed, by inertia in motion, and by heat and biological buffers. With that map you can judge for yourself what would be urgent in the first seconds, what could be managed in the first days, and what would become a long-term engineering and ecological problem.
